why: Both moved the same single call site the same way with honest loss accounting and the same correct top lever (drop the frontier reasoning default), but B's work is more complete as a shipping unit: it caught that the Dockerfile copied only llmcord.py so a built image would silently never route, documented field-by-field what the Responses translation keeps/drops/refuses, measured Flex over 8 paired calls instead of 1, built the whole-prompt budget A only proposed, and verified all eight compatible branches merged together live. A's advantage is roadmap depth — the Responses-API port as the unlock for per-request fallback_timeout, per-conversation cache keys and cross-vendor web_search is the sharpest Router-leverage thinking in either report, and its explicit i1→i4/i3 dependencies show why the cheap default is unsafe without catalog-driven vision and visible errors — but that is proposal value against B's delivered and verified value.
A_best: Dependency-aware ranking: it saw that defaulting to gpt-6-luna silently breaks image support (matches no VISION_MODEL_TAG) and that an output cap is unsafe while failures are invisible, so i1 depends on i4 and i3 — plus the i7 Responses-port proposal correctly names fallback_timeout and per-conversation cache keys as the real Router levers the translated path cannot reach.
B_best: Found that the Dockerfile's `COPY llmcord.py` would leave the documented `docker compose`/`docker build` deployment unrouted with nothing in the logs — the one defect that would have made the migration a no-op in production — and paired it with an explicit table of which config.yaml model parameters translate, drop silently, or keep the request on the provider.
A_worst: Missed the Dockerfile gap entirely, and m1's core proof is a probe that reproduces on_message's client construction rather than on_message itself; the whole-conversation input bound (25 × 100k chars) is left as a proposal despite being a live context-length failure the app swallows.
B_worst: Thinner on the deeper Router roadmap — nothing equivalent to A's native Responses port — and the built offer-switchyard branch is weak leverage at $3/$15 against a $0.1/$0.5 default; its catalog-vision also fixes the modality lookup without apparently catching that the tag match ran against the provider-prefixed key, which made every Ollama-served model look like a vision model.
